<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One Agent
<br class="ltx_break">From Narration to Long-Form Video</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chenyu Mu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Wenming Weng
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Qinrui Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Xingsong Ye
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hao Yu
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jun He
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chong Sun
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Chen Li
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jing LYU
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Erkun Yang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Cheng Deng
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>[
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions
that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use
multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost
trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear.
We address this gap with <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">WeVisCut</span>, a long-form script-to-video system
that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains
shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions
and repairs.
Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data
pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered
editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos,
this pipeline yields over <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">130K</span> training examples.
We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates
production and recovers from failures within the same harness.
Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing
quality and delivery reliability.
Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base
model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly
<span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">33<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.
It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<blockquote id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_quote">
<p id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“The whole eloquence of cinema is achieved in the editing
room.”</span></p>
<p id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_right"><span id="S1.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">— Orson Welles</span></p>
</blockquote>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Creating a narrated long-form video involves turning a script into a
sequence of coherent shots. Planning, visual retrieval, narration synthesis,
and timeline assembly are interdependent. Changing a shot’s duration affects
later timestamps, while unsuitable visual material may require both retrieval
and planning to be revisited across the affected shot sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recent agentic editors coordinate production through specialized agents and
tool workflows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. Several systems use general
models with feedback or graph refinement. Yet orchestration alone does not
specify how to train a compact policy that maintains video quality at low
token cost. Crayotter trains a 9B editing model using final-video preferences
on manually constructed tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>.
Such a policy needs a stateful environment for execution and recovery, together with
supervision grounded in that environment. Finished videos, however, omit the
tool calls, intermediate artifacts, and failures needed for such supervision.
The challenge is therefore
to connect stateful execution, executable supervision, and policy learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address these challenges, we present WeVisCut, which integrates a
script-to-video agent harness, executable data construction, and a task-adapted
policy. The harness (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) maintains shared production
state and validates tool actions. It exposes execution feedback for inspection,
bounded repair, and replanning while preserving unaffected artifacts
from earlier successful production steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Within this harness, we construct executable supervision through the
four-stage pipeline in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. We first recover script–shot
intent through editing inversion and execute it through verified replay.
When replay reveals defects, we apply observe–reflect–repair for bounded
corrections that preserve successful artifacts. We then use trajectory
materialization to organize the recorded executions into training examples
with tool feedback and repair outcomes. From 3,750 video projects, this
process yields over 130K examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Using these examples, we train a single 9B policy across production roles in
three phases (Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5 Training WeVisCut ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). In Phase 1, we establish tool use
and recovery through unified supervised fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>
and runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>.
In Phase 2, we apply Guided-OPD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> to learn recovery on
policy-reached states while phasing out teacher intervention.
In Phase 3, we use <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span>, our role- and context-factored
DAPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, to optimize decisions by comparing runtime outcomes
within matched roles and contexts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Moreover, we introduce a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks and five complementary
metrics to evaluate editing quality and delivery reliability. These metrics
relate rendered videos to their scripts and production plans, so evaluation
goes beyond successful rendering alone. In a shared tool environment, our
policy improves over its base model by <span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">16.0</span> points in Overall Score
and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly
<span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">33<math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.
Our complete system also outperforms task-matched native editors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize our contributions as follows.</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:12pt;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design a script-to-video agent harness that maintains shared
production state, validates tool actions, and supports inspection,
bounded repair, and final delivery.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build a four-stage data pipeline based on editing inversion and
verified replay, converting finished videos into executable training examples.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train a unified 9B policy for tool use and recovery through
sequential SFT, runtime-verified RFT, Guided-OPD, and <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span>
within a shared production harness.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics. WeVisCut improves
its base policy, outperforms task-matched systems, and achieves comparable
quality to Claude Opus 5 at markedly lower cost.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tool agents and long-horizon post-training.</span>
Producing long-form videos requires agents to choose tools and revise plans
from execution feedback. Earlier methods range from interleaved reasoning and
action <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> to learned API calls
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite> and runnable
tool dialogues <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>. To
train such behavior, researchers curate interactions and synthesize
instructions or tool calls <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>. Reflection and reusable skills also
support recovery <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. Closer to our
data pipeline, AgentTrek builds verified web trajectories from
tutorials <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>. Finished videos, however, do not record
editing actions. We therefore infer script–shot intent and replay it with
production tools to obtain executable trajectories. Long-horizon training
also needs to handle policy-generated states. DAgger <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> collects expert labels for
learner states, while generalized
knowledge distillation trains on student-generated sequences
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. Guided-OPD mixes teacher and student
turns, while TurnOPD and Step-Level OPD refine supervision at turn and step
boundaries <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. We apply
Guided-OPD with truncated teacher logits. For reward optimization, GRPO and
DAPO build on PPO-style updates with group-relative comparisons
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>. We adapt DAPO for
our multi-role policy as <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span>, comparing
rewards only within matched roles and decision contexts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Video editing.</span>
Video editing systems range from user-assisted tools to autonomous agents.
LAVE keeps users in the editing loop <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>. In more automated
settings, CutClaw and CineAgents handle music-synchronized editing and
cinematic compilation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.
The original Crayotter uses a traceable multi-agent workflow, while VideoAgent
assembles specialists dynamically <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>. Beyond
workflow design, task-specific training has also been explored. “The Script
is All You Need” trains a ScripterAgent but uses a separate DirectorAgent
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Aurora trains a planner for local edits
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite>. Building on the Crayotter environment, subsequent work
trains a 9B policy with final-video preferences on manually constructed
tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. In contrast, WeVisCut learns one role-routed
policy for fixed-narration production from executable trajectories built
through editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and
trajectory materialization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agent and video evaluation.</span>
Evaluation of narration-driven video production needs to consider both the
rendered video and the production process. VBench, VideoScore, and VMBench
assess generated-video quality and motion
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, while Goku-Bench
tests instruction-based edits <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. Script–video timing has
also been evaluated <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Complementary agent evaluation
ranges from recorded web and mobile trajectories
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite> to interactive shopping, browser,
and desktop environments that validate action outcomes
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. Software-repair benchmarks use repository
tests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, while multi-turn and tool-oriented suites
measure progress, valid transitions, and task constraints
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>.
We combine these perspectives in a benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks,
linking scripts, shot plans, tool trajectories, and rendered videos. Five
metrics are introduced to assess script fidelity, visual–narration alignment, timeline plan
realization, long-horizon consistency, and end-to-end delivery success.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>WeVisCut Agent Framework</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> presents the WeVisCut agent framework for long-form
script-to-video production. A shared policy makes editing decisions, while a
stateful runtime executes tools and maintains the resulting production
artifacts. Their interaction connects the narration script to a rendered video
through an inspectable process that supports revision when execution reveals
problems. We first define the task and policy–runtime interface, then describe
the harness that implements this process.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Script-to-Video Task</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A task input <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> consists of a fixed narration script <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, target aspect ratio
<math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, feasible duration interval <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>D</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, optional source assets, and a
versioned shared tool space <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. The goal is to render a video <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>
satisfying the delivery constraints without rewriting the narration. The
outputs also include a typed shot plan <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>, specifying narration coverage,
visual content, and timing, and an execution trajectory <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> recording calls
and returns throughout the production process (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Experimental Protocol and Reporting ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Production uses tools that accept typed arguments and return artifacts or
execution feedback. At call <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, a single policy <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> with shared
parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> serves a role <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{t}\in\{\mathrm{O},\mathrm{G},\mathrm{C}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{t}\in\{\mathrm{O},\mathrm{G},\mathrm{C}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The orchestrator (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{O}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>O</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{O}</annotation></semantics></math>) selects tools and arguments, the generator
(<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{G}</annotation></semantics></math>) supplies structured content, and the critic (<math id="S3.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{C}</annotation></semantics></math>)
inspects artifacts and requests or verifies repairs based on recorded execution feedback.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">At each call, the role context <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> combines the task input, role, a view of
the production state <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (shot plan, artifacts, and progress), relevant
call-and-return history <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, and tool schemas. The policy produces a complete
role output <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, which the runtime
<math id="S3.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math> processes under a tool contract <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="z_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),\qquad(o_{t},s_{t+1})\sim\mathcal{E}_{r_{t},u_{t}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},z_{t})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><msubsup><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),\qquad(o_{t},s_{t+1})\sim\mathcal{E}_{r_{t},u_{t}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},z_{t}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The contract specifies the tool, required fields, and value types. The runtime
returns observation <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, reporting results or blockers, and the updated
production state <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>. For orchestrator calls, the role output <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>
specifies a tool action <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> containing the selected tool and arguments
(Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38352v1/overview_harness.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/122;" width="476" height="122" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>The WeVisCut agent harness with stateful tool selection. A shared policy chooses legal
tools from the evolving production state. Validated returns update
artifacts and inform inspection, local repair, and replanning before
final stitching and delivery.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Harness Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The harness in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> implements the interaction in
Equation <a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> through a shared tool space, persistent production
state, and runtime checks. Each orchestrator turn selects one tool, which may
process multiple shots and invoke generator or critic calls. Tool selection
depends on the current production state, including available artifacts and blockers,
rather than a predetermined sequence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Production flow and tool system.</span>
Starting from the narration script <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, segmentation produces production
segments, and shot planning expands them into the shot plan <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math>. Shot records
connect narration spans to visual queries, target durations, and spotlight
assignments. Visual retrieval and text-to-speech (TTS) tools use these records
to obtain shot assets and narration audio. For spotlight shots, decoration
tools select verified <span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HyperFrames</span> templates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> and
fill typed slots, allowing the policy to control presentation through
structured content rather than raw layout code. Music search supplies
background music (BGM) for the final mix. Timeline composition combines shot
assets, narration audio, and decorations, while final rendering produces the
shot videos required for stitching. Quality judging and repair tools allow
the policy to revisit these intermediate products before delivery. This
progression describes artifact dependencies, not an obligatory ordering of
every tool call.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Persistent state and selective context.</span>
These tools communicate through the production state <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Global records
track narration coverage, shot order, and timing, while per-shot records
associate assets, audio, templates, renders, and unresolved issues with shot
IDs. Planned content remains distinct from artifacts that have actually been
produced. Episode memory retains these artifacts, and the event trace
preserves calls, returns, and failures. The initial observation exposes the
full production state. Subsequent role contexts <math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> contain the latest
runtime observation, state changes, a progress summary, and relevant local
records. Separating persistent storage from model context avoids repeatedly
serializing the entire project while preserving the information needed for
later inspection and repair.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Validated execution and actionable feedback.</span>
Given a tool action <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the runtime identifies the tool contract <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> and
checks argument schemas, artifact references, and execution prerequisites.
When structured content or inspection is required, it supplies this contract
in the generator’s or critic’s role context. Only the runtime commits
validated results to the production state, whereas
rejected calls return typed blockers that identify what must be corrected or
produced next. For example, a stitching request cannot substitute for missing
shot renders or background music. The runtime reports these missing
prerequisites, allowing the orchestrator to select the necessary production
tools before retrying. This separation keeps model decisions grounded in
execution evidence rather than treating a proposed plan as completed work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Artifact-grounded inspection and bounded repair.</span>
Execution feedback also determines when revision is needed. Quality inspection
combines structured checks of shot records, timing, and render status with a
VLM-Judge over spotlight renders. The critic identifies affected shots and the
defects that a repair should address. Repair tools then revise the relevant
content and recheck affected downstream artifacts while retaining still-valid
results. For example, correcting a decoration need not regenerate unchanged
narration audio. Repair limits bound repeated correction attempts, but
exhausting this budget does not remove the artifact prerequisites for delivery.
Quality warnings and missing production artifacts therefore remain distinct
conditions. The representative trajectory in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D A Representative Autonomous Tool-Use Flow ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>
illustrates how inspection, blocked calls, and targeted follow-up actions
interact within this loop.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verified delivery and trace retention.</span>
When the required artifacts are available, the policy requests final
stitching. Reaching the call limit also triggers a delivery attempt from the
available production state. Before stitching, the runtime checks the required
shot renders, narration audio, and background music. After stitching, it
validates the video and delivery manifest. Missing prerequisites are returned
as blockers while further calls are available. A run that terminates without a
validated final video is recorded as incomplete, with its execution trace
retained for diagnosis. The resulting production records support executable
data construction in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and policy training in
Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Training WeVisCut ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. This production harness is separate from the
read-only evaluation harness in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Evidence-Seeking Harness ‣ Appendix B Metrics and Evidence Protocol ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Data Construction</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The harness records execution, but finished videos expose only narration
and shot structure, not the tool calls, feedback, and repairs that produced
them. To train the shared policy, we recover editing intent and replay it
under the same state and action contract, constructing role-specific
examples grounded in real tool returns from executing the recovered intent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our source data consists of finished narration-driven videos collected from
Bilibili, spanning technology and digital products, business and finance,
natural science, and social sciences and humanities. The admitted set contains
3,750 video projects.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Executable Trajectory Construction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To convert these videos into executable supervision, we use a four-stage
pipeline comprising editing inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair,
and trajectory materialization (Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38352v1/figure_b_data_pipeline_Old.drawio.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/173;" width="476" height="173" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Executable data construction through editing
inversion, verified replay, observe–reflect–repair, and trajectory
materialization. (A) Editing inversion recovers aligned narration and shot
evidence from a finished video. (B) Verified replay executes this intent
with deployment-aligned production tools. (C) Observe–reflect–repair
performs bounded inspection and targeted repair to preserve successful
artifacts. (D) Trajectory materialization organizes recorded tool
interactions, feedback, and repair links into role-specific training
examples and rollout records.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Editing Inversion.</span>
We first recover script–shot intent from the source videos
(Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>A), including timestamped narration, shot structure, and
complete sentence–shot alignment for every admitted project. Narration
provides temporal anchors, while aligned shots indicate how the content is
organized visually. Together, this evidence forms a structured storyboard
describing what each shot should communicate, how long it should last, and
which production constraints it should satisfy. This process recovers the
intended video structure, not the original editor’s tool actions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Verified Replay.</span>
The recovered storyboard specifies what to produce, but does not provide
execution feedback. Verified replay (Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>B) therefore executes
this intent through a production toolchain aligned with the deployment state
and action contract.
Schema-checked tools maintain a shared production state across planning
(article segmentation, shot planning, and self-reflection), asset production
(visual retrieval with TTS, spotlight decoration, music search, and severity
ranking), and timeline execution (composition with judging, final rendering,
and stitching). Each real tool
return updates this state before the next decision. The runtime verifies
asset references, audio durations, template inputs, timeline positions, and
rendered outputs against the artifacts actually produced. Spotlight shots use
verified <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">HyperFrames</span> templates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite> that separate
layout, motion, and visual style. The policy selects a template and fills
typed slots instead of generating raw HTML, CSS, or JavaScript.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Observe–Reflect–Repair.</span>
During replay, quality inspection combines structured shot, timing,
decoration-slot, and render-status checks with a VLM-Judge over spotlight
renders. Using these inspection results, we locate production problems,
apply bounded local repairs supported by the toolchain, and verify these
changes while preserving successful artifacts (Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>C).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Trajectory Materialization.</span>
These executions produce trajectories that retain pre-action states, tool
names and arguments, real returns, created artifacts, quality verdicts, and
failure–repair links. Missing arguments, unresolved references, invalid stage
order, and failed delivery checks remain visible rather than being rewritten
as successes. We then organize these trajectories into role-specific examples
and rollout records (Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Executable Trajectory Construction ‣ 4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>D).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Training Examples and Data Split</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These examples provide role-specific supervision under the framework in
Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Orchestrator samples supervise tool selection and
structured arguments, while generator samples cover script segments, shot
plans, retrieval queries, and template content. Critic samples provide failure
localization, repair requests, and verification decisions. Runtime
observations remain context, with loss applied only to model-authored tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We partition by source project, keeping all its examples and repair
records together. Held-out projects supply the benchmark in
Section <a href="#S6.SS1" title="6.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.1</span></a> and are excluded from training. The
134,771 examples supervise a single Qwen3.5-9B policy with shared production
state and tool vocabulary across all three roles.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Training WeVisCut</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The executable examples provide initial supervision, but WeVisCut also needs
to handle the states produced by its own decisions. Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5 Training WeVisCut ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>
summarizes three training phases, comprising unified SFT and runtime-verified
RFT, recovery learning with Guided-OPD, and decision optimization with
<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span>. The policy interaction and agent harness are defined in
Section <a href="#S3" title="3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.38352v1/overview_algo.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/218;" width="476" height="218" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Three training phases of WeVisCut. Phase 1 learns tool use and
recovery through unified SFT and runtime-verified RFT. Phase 2 applies
Guided-OPD with decreasing teacher intervention. Phase 3 uses
<span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span> to compare alternatives within matched roles and decision
contexts.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Phase 1: Unified SFT and RFT</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> on the 134,771
examples constructed above. Following AgentTuning and
Agent-FLAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, we supervise model
responses while retaining tool feedback as input.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{\rm SFT}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{\rm SFT}</annotation></semantics></math> contain <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\rm SFT}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\rm SFT}</annotation></semantics></math> training examples.
We index examples by <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="e" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>e</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e</annotation></semantics></math> and tokens within an example by <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>.
The conversation <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{e}=(y_{e,1},\ldots,y_{e,L_{e}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{e}=(y_{e,1},\ldots,y_{e,L_{e}})</annotation></semantics></math> has <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{e}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{e}</annotation></semantics></math> tokens,
and <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{e,&lt;j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{e,&lt;j}</annotation></semantics></math> is the prefix before position <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math>. Before each response,
this prefix encodes the role context <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, including instructions and
available tool feedback. The loss mask <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{e,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{e,j}</annotation></semantics></math> is one for tokens in the
target model response and zero for instructions, tool-return messages, and
padding tokens added to equalize sequence lengths for batching. Thus only
response tokens contribute to the supervised fine-tuning loss</p>
<table id="S5.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\rm SFT}=-\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{e=1}^{N_{\rm SFT}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{e}}m_{e,j}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{e,j}\mid y_{e,&lt;j})}{\displaystyle\sum_{e=1}^{N_{\rm SFT}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{e}}m_{e,j}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover></mstyle><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>SFT</mi></msub></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover></mstyle><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\rm SFT}=-\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{e=1}^{N_{\rm SFT}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{e}}m_{e,j}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{e,j}\mid y_{e,&lt;j})}{\displaystyle\sum_{e=1}^{N_{\rm SFT}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_{e}}m_{e,j}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The denominator counts the supervised tokens, so the loss averages their
negative log probabilities across all supervised model responses in the corpus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">SFT teaches the recorded production steps, but the student can encounter
new failures when executing tasks on its own. We collect additional
supervision through runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning (RFT).
At the first recoverable failure, we restore the last replayable state before
the error and keep the valid earlier steps. The teacher regenerates the
complete remaining sequence from that state. Both student-only successes and
teacher-assisted repairs are replayed and admitted only if they pass the
runtime checks and a quality threshold selected on development tasks.
We track and balance these two sources of supervision. Failures that cannot
be restored enter a bounded pool for later rollout sampling.
Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Executable RFT and Guided-OPD ‣ Appendix A Optimization and Training Details ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> gives the admission rules for both sources of supervision.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Phase 2: Recovery Learning with Guided-OPD</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next apply Guided-OPD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>to learn decisions while interacting
with the production environment. At training update <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>, the teacher
generates a complete role output with probability <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the
student generates it with probability <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-\beta_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-\beta_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>. At call <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, we draw
<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\beta_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Bernoulli</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\beta_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> and use</p>
<table id="S5.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}\sim\begin{cases}\pi_{\phi}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),&amp;q_{t}=1,\\
\pi_{\theta}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),&amp;q_{t}=0\end{cases}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>ϕ</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>c</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}\sim\begin{cases}\pi_{\phi}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),&amp;q_{t}=1,\\
\pi_{\theta}^{(r_{t})}(\cdot\mid c_{t}),&amp;q_{t}=0\end{cases}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Here <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> is the frozen teacher’s parameter set. Both policies receive
the same role context <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. As in Equation <a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Script-to-Video Task ‣ 3 WeVisCut Agent Framework ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the complete
output <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is executed before the next call, when control is sampled again.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both branches train the student. Teacher outputs use forward KL against
the teacher distribution renormalized over its <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{\rm vocab}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>vocab</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{\rm vocab}</annotation></semantics></math> most likely
tokens, reducing the cost of distillation. Student outputs use reverse KL
on their own generated prefixes. We gradually reduce <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>β</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> from a
value below one to zero, so training ends with fully student-controlled
executions. Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Executable RFT and Guided-OPD ‣ Appendix A Optimization and Training Details ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a> specifies the token masks, KL losses,
and intervention schedule used throughout this training phase.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Phase 3: Decision Optimization with <span id="S5.SS3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span></h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we compare alternative outputs for the same production decision.
Our Role- and Context-Factored DAPO (<span id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span>) adapts
DAPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite> by restricting reward comparisons to the same role
and production context. At a fixed role call, we sample candidate outputs
<math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="z_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">z_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> indexes alternatives in the comparison group. For example,
generator candidates may be different retrieval queries for the same shot.
For orchestrator calls, we restore the
same production state, sample alternative next actions, and execute each
with a frozen continuation policy, the same tool registry, budget, and
paired random seeds. Generator and critic outputs are evaluated under the
same local request, artifact, and tool contract.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Each candidate receives a role-specific reward <math id="S5.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{i}^{(r)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{i}^{(r)}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Orchestrator rewards combine successful delivery and final quality with
partial credit for persistent progress on failed executions. Generator
rewards assess schema validity, requirement coverage, and content usability.
Critic rewards assess diagnosis, repair utility, and verification, with a
penalty for unnecessary repairs. The scoring rules, rubrics, and weights
are fixed. Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Role- and Context-Factored DAPO ‣ Appendix A Optimization and Training Details ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> defines the complete reward formulas.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Within a group with matching conditions <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math>, we convert rewards into
relative advantages</p>
<table id="S5.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}^{(r)}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\frac{R_{i}^{(r)}-\mu_{\kappa}^{(r)}}{\sigma_{\kappa}^{(r)}+\epsilon}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.812em;" width="0.812em"><mi>sg</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>μ</mi><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}^{(r)}=\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\frac{R_{i}^{(r)}-\mu_{\kappa}^{(r)}}{\sigma_{\kappa}^{(r)}+\epsilon}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu_{\kappa}^{(r)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>μ</mi><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu_{\kappa}^{(r)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{\kappa}^{(r)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{\kappa}^{(r)}</annotation></semantics></math> are the group’s mean
reward and standard deviation, <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> prevents division by zero,
and <math id="S5.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{sg}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>sg</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{sg}</annotation></semantics></math> stops gradients through the advantages.
Above-mean rewards yield positive advantages, and below-mean rewards yield
negative ones. Groups with insufficient
reward variation are resampled, with quotas and a replay queue maintaining
coverage. Contexts are collected from the current policy with gradients
stopped, and role losses are balanced after token-level normalization.
We retain DAPO’s asymmetric Clip-Higher and soft overlong shaping.
Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Role- and Context-Factored DAPO ‣ Appendix A Optimization and Training Details ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> details the sampling and updates.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate whether task-specific training improves script-to-video production
and whether these gains extend to complete editing systems. We first compare
policies in a shared tool environment, then compare WeVisCut with editors using
their native workflows. Separating these comparisons distinguishes policy
performance from differences in tools and orchestration. We further examine
the cumulative training stages and assess the rendered videos through blinded
human evaluation.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmark and implementation.</span>
We construct a fixed benchmark of 100 script-to-video tasks from the held-out
source projects in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Data Construction ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Each task specifies a
narration script, source pool, target duration, and aspect ratio. All systems
receive identical task inputs and delivery constraints. Our
trainable variants share the Qwen3.5-9B backbone, training split, decoding
configuration, tool registry, and rendering budget. The Guided-OPD and
<span id="S6.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">RCF-DAPO</span> training configurations are given in Appendix
Table <a href="#A1.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ A.2 Role- and Context-Factored DAPO ‣ Appendix A Optimization and Training Details ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison methods.</span>
For the policy comparison, all models use the same instructions, tool schemas,
runtime, and rendering budget. We evaluate Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.6-27B, and
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, together with
Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Gemini 3.1 Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, and a fixed
Claude Opus 5 snapshot. These reference models receive no task-specific
post-training. Our variants differ only in the training stages applied to the
shared 9B backbone within the same production environment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare WeVisCut with Crayotter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> and the
commentary-capable VideoAgent workflow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, each using
its released tools and orchestration. Adapters may translate file formats and
export evaluation artifacts, but may not retrieve assets, write narration,
create plans, or repair outputs. CutClaw, CineAgents, and
DirectorAgent <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> are
excluded from this quantitative comparison because their native workflows
omit or replace parts of the fixed-narration, fixed-source task contract.
Appendix Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.1 External Baseline Contract ‣ Appendix C Experimental Protocol and Reporting ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> shows whether each system
supports the required inputs, shot plans, and execution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation metrics.</span>
We propose five complementary metrics for script-to-video production that
assess the relationship between the source script, editing plan, execution
trace, and rendered video. All scores lie in <math id="S6.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,100]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0,100</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,100]</annotation></semantics></math>, with higher values
indicating better performance. Script Content Fidelity (SCF) measures
the coverage, faithfulness, and ordering of narration claims relative to the
source script. Visual–Narration Semantic Match (VNSM) assesses whether
rendered visuals support the concurrent narration. Timeline Plan Realization
(TPR) compares planned and realized shots in presence, duration, and order.
Long-Horizon Consistency (LHC) measures late-stage shot-health retention and
asset diversity. End-to-End Rendering Yield (ERY) is the fraction of held-out
tasks producing a decodable, sufficiently complete video with the required
non-silent narration. Overall Score is the equally weighted mean of the five
reported metric means, used only as a descriptive summary
for comparing aggregate task performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Production Cost Efficiency (PCE) is reported separately as tool calls and
generated tokens per successful output minute. For native systems, we instead
report wall-clock minutes and estimated USD per successful output minute,
since the underlying tools and services differ. Both measures include failed
attempts in the cost numerator, and lower values are better. Definitions,
eligibility rules, and missing-data treatment are given in
Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Metrics and Evidence Protocol ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation protocol.</span>
Each system is evaluated in five independent runs over the 100 tasks. We
report across-run means and standard deviations for the five component
metrics, with no uncertainty estimate for Overall Score. Permissions and
retry limits are fixed within the shared environment, and thresholds,
adapters, and evaluator settings are selected on development tasks.
Semantic evaluation uses timestamped contact sheets in a read-only,
network-free environment with access restricted to metric-specific evidence.
The held-out evaluator, its prompts, and the five reported metrics are not
used as post-SFT training signals. The metric-validation protocol is described
in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Diagnostic Validation ‣ Appendix B Metrics and Evidence Protocol ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, and evidence collection and
isolation within the read-only evaluation environment are detailed in
Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Evidence-Seeking Harness ‣ Appendix B Metrics and Evidence Protocol ‣ WeVisCut: The Whole Editing Room in One AgentFrom Narration to Long-Form Video" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Policy Comparison</h3>

full test set. Overall is the equal-weight mean of the five component means.
Calls and generated tokens include all attempts and are normalized by
